---
title: "Figure 1.2.3: CA4: Enforcement Impact on Remittance Growth"
---

![Python: `python/fig-1-2-3.py`](../images/python/fig-1-2-3.png)

An event-study chart: the estimated response of remittance growth to
Central America (CA4) in the six months before and after a change in US
immigration enforcement. Month 0 is the shock. The line is the estimated
effect and the shaded area its 90 percent confidence interval. Where the
band includes zero, the effect is not statistically significant. The months
before the shock serve as a check: there, the estimated effect should be
close to zero.

**New in this chart:**

- negative x-values (months before the shock);
- a dotted line marking the shock;
- tick marks only where they do not collide with that line;
- an x-axis title.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 13 rows (months -6 to 6):

| category | ci_lo | range | coef |
|---|---|---|---|
| -6 | -6.78 | 15.58 | 1.66 |

- `coef` is the estimated effect, drawn as the line.
- `ci_lo` is the lower edge of the confidence interval.
- `range` is the width of the band, stacked on top of `ci_lo` in Excel, as
  in other band charts. The upper edge is `ci_lo + range`.

The `category` column holds the months as numbers, from -6 to 6, so they can
go on a numeric x-axis directly. Negative x-values need no special
treatment.

## The script

### The band edges

```python
months = data["category"]

# In Excel the confidence band is a stacked area: "ci_lo" plus "range".
ci_lower = data["ci_lo"]
ci_upper = data["ci_lo"] + data["range"]
```

The upper edge is computed once and given a name, so the drawing code reads
naturally. See [Shaded bands](../techniques.qmd#sec-bands).

### The frame

`new_chart()` is called with `title_size=13.5`, half a point larger than the
default, as in the published chart. `bottom_gap=0.5` is larger than usual,
because below the month labels there is also an axis title.

### The band

```python
ax.fill_between(months, ci_lower, ci_upper, color="#FCE4D4", alpha=0.9, linewidth=0)
```

A pale orange band from the lower to the upper edge. `alpha=0.9` makes it
very slightly transparent, which on a white background just makes it a
touch lighter. `linewidth=0` removes the outline. The band is drawn first,
so everything after it lies on top.

### The axis line and the shock

```python
# The x-axis is drawn at zero, with short tick marks pointing up, and a
# dotted line marks the month of the shock.
ax.axhline(0, color="#333333", linewidth=0.9)
ax.vlines(months[months != 0], 0, 0.55, color="#333333", linewidth=0.7)
ax.axvline(0, color="#111111", linewidth=1.0, linestyle=(0, (1, 1.5)))
```

The horizontal axis is drawn at zero, in the middle of the plot, while the
month labels stay at the bottom. See [An axis line at
zero](../techniques.qmd#sec-axis-line).

- **The tick marks** are short vertical lines from 0 to 0.55, one per month.
  The height is in data units: 0.55 on a range of 30 (-15 to 15) is about
  2 percent of the plot height.
- **No tick at the shock.** `months[months != 0]` keeps all months except
  month 0, because there the dotted vertical line takes the place of the
  tick. This is the pandas way of filtering: `months != 0` gives a column of
  `True` and `False`, and putting it in square brackets keeps the values
  where it is `True`.
- **The dotted line.** `ax.axvline(0, ...)` draws a vertical line across the
  full height of the plot at month 0. `linestyle=(0, (1, 1.5))` gives short
  dots with slightly longer gaps; the lengths are in line widths. See [Line
  styles](../techniques.qmd#sec-line-styles).

### The estimate

```python
ax.plot(months, data["coef"], color="#C85C0A", linewidth=2.2,
        solid_capstyle="round", solid_joinstyle="round")
```

The estimate is drawn last, so it lies on top of the band and the axis
lines. It is a thick (2.2 points) dark orange line, the same hue as the
band. Round caps and joins avoid sharp corners at each month.

### The axes

```python
ax.set_xlim(-6, 6)
ax.set_xticks(range(-6, 7))
ax.set_xlabel("Months relative to shock", fontsize=9, labelpad=7)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0, pad=5)

ax.set_ylim(-15, 15)
ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(MultipleLocator(5))
ax.tick_params(axis="y", direction="in", length=2.5, pad=5)
```

- **The x-axis** runs exactly from -6 to 6, so the line and the band start
  and end at the edges of the plot.
- **Ticks.** `range(-6, 7)` is -6, -5, ..., 6, a label for every month. A
  Python `range` stops *before* its second number, hence the 7.
- **The axis title.** `ax.set_xlabel()` writes a title under the labels.
  `labelpad=7` puts 7 points between the labels and the title. Most REO
  charts have no axis titles, because the subtitle gives the unit; here the
  x-axis needs one, since "months relative to shock" is not obvious from the
  numbers alone.
- **The bottom spine** and its tick marks are hidden, because the axis line
  is now at zero.
- **The y-axis** runs from -15 to 15 with a tick every 5, symmetric around
  zero. The ticks point inwards (`direction="in"`).

There is no legend. The caption explains the band.

## Changing the chart

- **Mark the shock with a label.** Add
  `ax.text(0.2, 14, "Shock", fontsize=8, fontstyle="italic", va="top")`,
  just to the right of the dotted line, near the top.
- **A longer window.** For months -12 to 12, change the limits to
  `(-12, 12)` and label every second month: `range(-12, 13, 2)`. The
  `months != 0` filter keeps working.
- **A line at the band edges.** Some event-study charts outline the
  interval instead of shading it: `ax.plot(months, ci_lower, linestyle="--")`
  and the same for `ci_upper`.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-1-2-3.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-1-2-3.py"}
"""Figure 1.2.3: CA4: Enforcement Impact on Remittance Growth."""
from matplotlib.ticker import MultipleLocator

from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart

STEM = "fig-1-2-3"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)
months = data["category"]

# In Excel the confidence band is a stacked area: "ci_lo" plus "range".
ci_lower = data["ci_lo"]
ci_upper = data["ci_lo"] + data["range"]

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="CA4: Enforcement Impact on Remittance Growth",
    subtitle="(Percentage points)",
    caption=(
        "Source: IMF staff calculations.\n"
        "Note: Estimated response of remittance growth to changes in immigration\n"
        "enforcement based on panel local projections (Carare and others\n"
        "(forthcoming)). Regressions include country and time fixed effects and\n"
        "macroeconomic controls. Shaded area denotes 90 percent wild cluster\n"
        "bootstrap confidence intervals."
    ),
    title_size=13.5,
    left=0.4,
    right=0.2,
    bottom_gap=0.5,
)

ax.fill_between(months, ci_lower, ci_upper, color="#FCE4D4", alpha=0.9, linewidth=0)

# The x-axis is drawn at zero, with short tick marks pointing up, and a
# dotted line marks the month of the shock.
ax.axhline(0, color="#333333", linewidth=0.9)
ax.vlines(months[months != 0], 0, 0.55, color="#333333", linewidth=0.7)
ax.axvline(0, color="#111111", linewidth=1.0, linestyle=(0, (1, 1.5)))

ax.plot(months, data["coef"], color="#C85C0A", linewidth=2.2,
        solid_capstyle="round", solid_joinstyle="round")

ax.set_xlim(-6, 6)
ax.set_xticks(range(-6, 7))
ax.set_xlabel("Months relative to shock", fontsize=9, labelpad=7)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0, pad=5)

ax.set_ylim(-15, 15)
ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(MultipleLocator(5))
ax.tick_params(axis="y", direction="in", length=2.5, pad=5)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
